item.title: CFM Week 33 — Job: Yet Will I Trust in Him
item.description: A 03:29:15 doctrinal deep dive on the book of Job — the hardest book in the Old Testament, and the one that takes the most comforting thing we believe about the universe and puts it on trial. The reading is Job 1–3; 12–14; 19; 21–24; 38–40; 42. We begin with the shape of the book, because being lost about the structure makes you misread everything: a plain prose frame at each end and thirty-nine chapters of dense poetry in between — and the Job of the frame is serene while the Job of the poetry is in agony. Both are canonical. We show that the question driving the book is not “why do the righteous suffer?” but the adversary’s question in 1:9, “Doth Job fear God for nought?” — can anyone love God for nothing? We look hard at the Hebrew: ha-satan, “the accuser,” a courtroom title; tam, “perfect,” meaning whole rather than sinless; and chinnam, the word the accuser uses for “for nought” that God turns back in 2:3 to say Job was destroyed “without cause.” A full section asks where “the patience of Job” came from, and the answer is startling: James wrote hypomone, endurance, not serenity — and the Greek Job the early church actually read is about one-sixth shorter than the Hebrew, with the deepest cuts falling exactly where Job argues most fiercely. Origen noticed it in the third century. We meet Gregory the Great, who knew Job’s angry speeches scandalized readers and answered them; the Testament of Job, which sands off every hard edge; the Talmud’s Rava, who ruled that “a person is not held responsible for what he says when he is in distress”; and President John Taylor, who said plainly in 1859, “I do not think he was a very patient man… who would not be?” We handle two hard verses honestly — the ketiv/qere of 13:15 behind this week’s title, and the italics in 19:26 that show “worms” was supplied by the KJV translators and is not in the Hebrew — and we set the go’el, the kinsman-redeemer legally bound by blood to take up your cause, next to the Redeemer who made Himself our relative. Then the whirlwind, where God asks seventy questions and explains nothing; Behemoth and Leviathan, because God’s comfort is not that the world is safe but that nothing in it is unowned; and chapter 42, where God’s wrath is kindled not against the man who shouted but against the three who defended Him — the theology Elder Boyd K. Packer named from the pulpit in April 1991 as “false doctrine.” The animals come back doubled; the children do not, and that arithmetic is the whole doctrine of the Resurrection. We close in Liberty Jail, where D&C 121 opens “O God, where art thou?” and the Lord answers “My son, peace be unto thy soul… thou art not yet as Job” — and where D&C 122:8 finally supplies the daysman Job asked for in 9:33 and never received: “The Son of Man hath descended below them all.” Joseph Smith called W. W. Phelps “one of Job’s comforters” from that jail, and then forgave him — and Phelps went on to write “Praise to the Man.” Drawn from the full Gospel Library: scripture, General Conference 1971–April 2026, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Journal of Discourses, the Joseph Smith Papers, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, and the Babylonian and Egyptian literature of the righteous sufferer.
item.itunes:summary: A 03:29:15 deep dive on Job. The driving question is not “why do the righteous suffer?” but the accuser’s question in 1:9 — “Doth Job fear God for nought?” Can anyone love God for nothing? We take the book’s structure apart, sit with chapter 3 without flinching, and show why the friends were superb for seven silent days and destructive the moment they spoke. Where did “the patience of Job” come from? James wrote hypomone — endurance, not silence — and the Greek Job the early church read was one-sixth shorter than the Hebrew, trimmed most where Job argues hardest. We handle the hard verses honestly: the two readings preserved in 13:15, and the KJV italics in 19:26 showing “worms” is not in the Hebrew. The go’el of 19:25 is a kinsman legally bound by blood — which is why the Redeemer had to become our relative. Then the whirlwind, Behemoth and Leviathan, and chapter 42, where God rebukes the friends and not the man who shouted. The livestock come back doubled; the ten children do not — and that is the Resurrection in arithmetic. Closes in Liberty Jail: “O God, where art thou?” answered by “My son, peace be unto thy soul… thou art not yet as Job,” and the daysman of Job 9:33 finally named in D&C 122:8.

item.title: CFM Week 32 — Esther: Thou Art Come … for Such a Time as This
item.description: A 2h51m doctrinal deep dive on the whole book of Esther — all ten chapters — and on the strangest fact in the Old Testament: this is the one book that never says God’s name. Not once. No “LORD,” no “God,” no prayer, no temple, no covenant, no altar, no prophet, no miracle. The people are never even called “Israel,” only “the Jews.” And yet it is the book the Church quotes most often when someone is asked to do something frightening. The whole episode turns on that tension. We open in Persia — Shushan the palace, Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) and his 180-day feast — and with the Jews who did not go home: last week’s Ezra and Nehemiah followed the returning remnant, and Esther follows the ones who stayed in the empire. Same century, opposite choice. We read Vashti honestly, meet Hadassah the orphan with two names, and sit with Mordecai at the gate day after day, faithful where he can do nothing. Then Haman the Agagite — and the Amalek thread running back through 1 Samuel 15 to Exodus 17, the enemy Saul the Benjamite failed to finish now standing over Saul’s Benjamite kinsman. Genocide by paperwork: the lot, the ring, the posts riding out, and “the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed” (3:15). At the heart is chapter 4 — the thirty days, the golden sceptre, and Mordecai’s three great moves: think not that thou shalt escape; deliverance will arise “from another place”; “who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” Even the rescue’s source goes unnamed. No prayer is recorded — but a fast is, three days, night and day (4:16), and a fast is a prayer with a body. “If I perish, I perish” is set beside “but if not” (Daniel 3:18) and “nevertheless” in Gethsemane. Then the sleepless night of chapter 6 — seven words that turn the book — and an ending with no hymn, only a festival. A full section traces how this book has been read for 2,500 years, and the last section brings it home to the Latter-day Saints: Joseph Smith writing from Liberty Jail in December 1838, seven weeks after Missouri’s extermination order — “we want you to remember Haman and Mordecai” — and Lorenzo Snow in General Conference, October 1882, six months after the Edmunds Act, calling the sisters to “act the part of Esther, the queen.” Across all twenty-six volumes of the Journal of Discourses there is exactly one discourse on Esther. It is not a devotional book for the early Saints. It is a crisis text — and it surfaces both times the Saints are living under a written government decree. Drawn from the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Journal of Discourses, the Interpreter Foundation, the Greek Additions of the Septuagint, and the Jewish historian Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 31 — Ezra 1; 3–7; Nehemiah 2; 4–6; 8: I Am Doing a Great Work
item.description: A 3h06m doctrinal deep dive on Ezra 1; 3–7 and Nehemiah 2; 4–6; 8 — the story of a people who came home to ruins and built anyway. It opens with an empire moved by God: “the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” (Ezra 1:1), fulfilling Jeremiah’s seventy years and releasing the exiles with the temple vessels restored by inventory. In Ezra 3 the returning remnant sets up the altar first, before a single foundation stone is laid — worship precedes construction — and when the foundation is finally laid, the old men who had seen the first house weep aloud while the young shout for joy, “so that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping” (Ezra 3:12–13). Then comes opposition: adversaries offer to help, are refused, and write letters that stop the work for years — until Haggai and Zechariah stir the people up again, Darius searches the royal archives, finds Cyrus’s original roll, and the very empire that halted the temple ends up funding it (Ezra 4–6). Ezra 7 gives the hinge of the whole book: “Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments” (7:10) — seek, do, teach, in that order. Nehemiah then takes up the wall: a cupbearer’s sadness before the king, a prayer prayed in the space between a question and its answer (2:4), a night ride among the rubble, and “Let us rise up and build” (2:18). Sanballat and Tobiah mock — “will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish?” (4:2) — the builders work with a tool in one hand and a sword in the other, trusting that “our God shall fight for us” (4:20), and Nehemiah confronts a wound from within when the people charge each other interest (ch. 5). Four times he is invited down to the plain of Ono, and four times he answers the line that titles the week: “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down” (6:3). The wall is finished in “fifty and two days” (6:15). It ends at the Water Gate, where the people ask for the book, Ezra reads from morning until midday, the Levites “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (8:8), and to a weeping congregation comes the word that carries the whole restoration: “the joy of the LORD is your strength” (8:10). Drawn from the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Journal of Discourses, the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 3h06m deep dive on Ezra 1; 3–7 and Nehemiah 2; 4–6; 8 — rebuilding under opposition. God stirs up Cyrus to send the exiles home (Ezra 1:1); the altar goes up before the foundation; and when the foundation is laid, shouting and weeping blend until no one “could discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping” (3:12–13). Enemies stall the temple for years until Haggai and Zechariah stir the work up again and Darius’s archive search turns Cyrus’s lost decree into imperial funding (Ezra 4–6). Ezra 7:10 supplies the pattern for every disciple: prepare the heart to seek, to do, and to teach. Nehemiah surveys the ruins by night, says “Let us rise up and build” (2:18), absorbs mockery about reviving “the stones out of the heaps of rubbish” (4:2), builds with sword and trowel, and refuses four invitations to the plain of Ono with the line that names the week: “I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down” (6:3). The wall stands in fifty and two days. At the Water Gate the Levites “gave the sense” of the law (8:8) and a weeping people are told, “the joy of the LORD is your strength” (8:10).

item.title: CFM Week 30 — 2 Chronicles 14–20; 26; 30: Our Eyes Are upon Thee
item.description: A 4h02m doctrinal deep dive on 2 Chronicles 14–20; 26; 30 — four kings of Judah (Asa, Jehoshaphat, Uzziah, and Hezekiah) bound together by one Hebrew verb, darash, “to seek.” The Chronicler states the promise once and proves it again and again: “if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you” (2 Chronicles 15:2). It is framed by a two-way gaze — the eyes of the Lord that “run to and fro throughout the whole earth” to strengthen the faithful (16:9), and our own eyes lifted to Him when we have no might and know not what to do (20:12). First, Asa (2 Chronicles 14–16): he seeks the Lord and defeats Zerah’s vast host — “we rest on thee” (14:11) — then, when strong, leans on a Syrian alliance instead of God, jails the seer, and in disease “sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians” (16:12); seeking is a posture, not a single act. Second, Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 17–20): he teaches the law city to city, stumbles into alliance with Ahab (Micaiah’s lone courage, ch.18), then, surrounded by armies, proclaims a fast and prays the prayer that titles the week — “we have no might… neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee” (20:12) — and watches God fight the battle for him: “the battle is not yours, but God’s” (20:15). Third, Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26): “as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper” (26:5), but “when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction” (26:16) — he seizes the priest’s office and is struck with leprosy; pride is the sin of the strong. Fourth, Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 30): he reopens the temple and invites even the scattered northern remnant to the Passover, and when many come unprepared he prays, “The good LORD pardon every one that prepareth his heart to seek God” (30:18–19) — and the Lord heals the people; mercy gathers. Throughout, the question is personal: how do we keep seeking the Lord in strength as well as in extremity? Drawn from the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Journal of Discourses, the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h02m deep dive on 2 Chronicles 14–20; 26; 30, built on one Hebrew verb — darash, “to seek” — and the promise of 2 Chronicles 15:2: “if ye seek him, he will be found of you.” Four kings of Judah test it. Asa rests on God against Zerah’s host (“we rest on thee,” 14:11) but late in life trusts a Syrian alliance and the physicians instead of the Lord. Jehoshaphat, surrounded by armies, fasts and prays the prayer that titles the week — “we have no might… but our eyes are upon thee” (20:12) — and learns “the battle is not yours, but God’s” (20:15). Uzziah prospers while he seeks the Lord, then in strength grows proud, seizes the priest’s office, and is struck with leprosy (26:5,16). Hezekiah reopens the temple and prays that the Lord will pardon everyone who “prepareth his heart to seek God” (30:18–19). Seeking is a posture, not a single act. item.title: CFM Week 29 — 2 Kings 16–25: He Trusted in the Lord God of Israel
item.description: A 2h54m doctrinal deep dive on 2 Kings 16–25 — the long descent of the two kingdoms and the one virtue that outlasts them all: “He trusted in the Lord God of Israel; so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor any that were before him” (2 Kings 18:5, of Hezekiah). Six movements. First, Ahaz at the crossroads (2 Kings 16): a king of Judah who, offered a sign from heaven, chooses instead to trust Assyria, strips the temple to pay tribute, and copies a pagan altar from Damascus — trust misplaced. Second, the fall of the Northern Kingdom (2 Kings 17): after two centuries of ripening apostasy, Israel is carried away by Assyria, and the chapter pauses to explain exactly why — “because they obeyed not the voice of the Lord their God” — the sober theology behind the scattering of the ten tribes and the resettlement that produced the Samaritans. Third, Hezekiah and the God who saves (2 Kings 18–19): Sennacherib's army at the gate, the Rabshakeh's psychological siege of taunts against the wall of Jerusalem, Hezekiah spreading the threatening letter before the Lord in the temple, Isaiah's word of deliverance, and one night in which the camp of Assyria is emptied — trust vindicated. Fourth, illness and a fatal welcome (2 Kings 20–21): Hezekiah healed and given fifteen added years and the sign of the sundial turned back, then his proud display of the treasury to Babylon's envoys — and the long shadow of his son Manasseh, the most wicked and longest-reigning king of Judah. Fifth, Josiah and the great reformation (2 Kings 22–23): a boy king, the book of the law rediscovered in the temple, the prophetess Huldah consulted, a covenant renewed, the idols purged, and the greatest Passover since the days of the judges — proof that revival is possible even late. And sixth, the fall of Judah and the mercy hidden in judgment (2 Kings 24–25): Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah; the Babylonian siege; the burning of Jerusalem and the temple; the exile — set against the Book of Mormon's own opening, for Lehi leaves Jerusalem “in the first year of the reign of Zedekiah” (1 Nephi 1:4), the same king and the same crisis. The book closes not in darkness but with Jehoiachin lifted from prison and seated at the king's table — a small, deliberate ember of hope carried into captivity. Throughout, the question is personal: what it means to trust in the Lord God of Israel while the world around us declines. Drawn from the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Journal of Discourses, the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 2h54m deep dive on 2 Kings 16–25, built on one line about Hezekiah: “He trusted in the Lord God of Israel” (2 Kings 18:5). Six movements — Ahaz trusts Assyria instead of the sign of heaven (ch 16); the Northern Kingdom falls and the text explains why (ch 17); Hezekiah spreads Sennacherib's letter before the Lord and the Assyrian camp is emptied overnight (ch 18–19); Hezekiah is healed with the sundial's sign, then Manasseh's long wickedness follows (ch 20–21); young Josiah finds the book of the law and leads the greatest reformation and Passover since the judges (ch 22–23); and Judah falls to Babylon — the same crisis that opens the Book of Mormon, “the first year of the reign of Zedekiah” (1 Nephi 1:4) — yet the book ends on an ember of hope with Jehoiachin lifted from prison (ch 24–25). Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: Doctrinal Study — The Eternal Regress? Lorenzo Snow's Couplet and Infinite Regression
item.description: A 34-minute doctrinal study of one of the most discussed sentences in Latter-day Saint thought: Lorenzo Snow's couplet, “As man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may become.” The study walks the scripture chain behind the doctrine of deification and eternal progression, then follows B. H. Roberts' rigorous line of reasoning on the infinite regression of Gods — an “endless line” of divine beings stretching back without beginning — as he developed it in A New Witness for God and The Mormon Doctrine of Deity. It then sets that reasoning honestly against credible voices that take a contrary position, including Blake Ostler's case for monarchotheism, Elder Bruce R. McConkie's warning in “The Seven Deadly Heresies,” and the measured reticence of official sources such as the Gospel Topics essay “Becoming Like God” and President Gordon B. Hinckley's public remarks. The aim is not to settle the question but to map it faithfully: what the scriptures affirm, what a careful Latter-day Saint thinker argued, where thoughtful disciples have disagreed, and where the Church has chosen to speak with deliberate restraint. Every quotation is drawn from verified primary sources.
item.itunes:summary: A 34-minute study of Lorenzo Snow's couplet — “As man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may become” — and the question of infinite regression. A faithful map of what is affirmed, what is argued, and where the Church speaks with deliberate reticence. All quotations from verified primary sources.

item.title: CFM Week 28 — 2 Kings 2–7: There Is a Prophet in Israel
item.description: A 3h38m doctrinal deep dive on 2 Kings 2–7 — the heart of the Elisha cycle, built on one sentence a prophet sends to a foreign general: “Let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel” (2 Kings 5:8). Where Elijah was a prophet of fire, drought, and judgment, Elisha — whose name means “God saves,” from the same Hebrew root behind the name of Jesus — is a prophet of grace, restoration, and abundance, and nearly every miracle bends toward mercy. Six movements. First, the mantle passes (2 Kings 2): Elijah and Elisha retrace Israel’s conquest route in reverse; three times Elijah says “tarry here” and three times Elisha refuses; he asks for “a double portion” — the firstborn’s inheritance, a claim to be true heir — sees the chariot of fire, takes up the fallen cloak, and parts the Jordan, and the sons of the prophets confess, “The spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha.” Second, water in the desert (2 Kings 3): righteous Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there not here a prophet of the Lord?” and the promise of water arrives before any wind or rain. Third, provision and resurrection (2 Kings 4): the widow’s pot of oil that fills every borrowed vessel, the Shunammite’s son raised from death, the poisoned pottage healed, and a hundred fed from twenty barley loaves — a clear prototype of Christ’s own feeding and raising miracles. Fourth, Naaman cleansed and Gehazi cursed (2 Kings 5): a captive Israelite maid points the leprous Syrian to the prophet; Naaman rages at the plainness of “wash seven times in Jordan,” then obeys and comes up clean “like unto the flesh of a little child,” while Gehazi chases the reward and inherits the leprosy — the power of God is never for sale, and grace reaches the humble outsider (the very text Jesus cited at Nazareth, Luke 4:27). Fifth, the axe head and the fiery host (2 Kings 6): iron made to swim, Syria’s raids foiled, and at Dothan the servant’s eyes opened to “the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire” — “they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” And sixth, the four lepers and the lifted siege (2 Kings 7): outcasts expecting to die become the first bearers of good tidings as the Lord empties the Syrian camp overnight, and every word of the prophet comes to pass — blessing the believing, condemning the scornful. Throughout, Elisha stands as a type of Christ — “God saves” in name and in deed — and as the scriptural charter (with Doctrine and Covenants 121:36–37) that the priesthood cannot be handled for gain or pride. Drawn from the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Journal of Discourses, the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 3h38m deep dive on 2 Kings 2–7, the Elisha cycle, around one sentence: “there is a prophet in Israel” (2 Kings 5:8). Elijah’s mantle passes to Elisha — “God saves” — a prophet of grace whose miracles bend toward mercy: water in the desert, the widow’s oil, the Shunammite’s son raised, poisoned pottage healed, a hundred fed from twenty loaves. Naaman the Syrian is cleansed by obeying the plain word “wash seven times in Jordan” while greedy Gehazi inherits his leprosy; iron is made to swim; at Dothan the servant’s eyes open to horses and chariots of fire — “they that be with us are more”; and four lepers become bearers of good tidings when the Lord lifts the siege of Samaria overnight. Elisha as a type of Christ. Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 27 — 1 Kings 12–13; 17–22: If the Lord Be God, Follow Him
item.description: A 4h00m doctrinal deep dive on 1 Kings 12–13 and 17–22 — a kingdom learning the hardest lesson in scripture: you cannot serve two gods. After Solomon's death the united monarchy fractures, the northern kingdom sinks into Baal worship under Ahab and Jezebel, and into that darkness God sends Elijah the Tishbite, whose name means "Jehovah is my God." The week turns on one ultimatum: "How long halt ye between two opinions? if the Lord be God, follow him" (1 Kings 18:21) — where the Hebrew picture behind "halt" is not stopping but limping, trying to walk two directions at once and going nowhere. Five movements. The first is the kingdom divided (1 Kings 12–13): Rehoboam rejects the elders' counsel of servant-leadership for his peers' threat of "scorpions," ten tribes secede, Jeroboam erects golden calves at Dan and Bethel, and a man of God is undone by a false claim of angelic revelation — a sobering lesson on holding to the clear word God gives. The second is Elijah and the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17): a drought "according to my word" challenges Baal the supposed god of rain, and God sustains His prophet by a destitute Gentile widow in Jezebel's own homeland — "make me thereof a little cake first" — the barrel of meal that wastes not, and the first raising of the dead in scripture. The third is the spine of the week, Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18): 450 prophets of Baal cry and cut themselves with no answer, Elijah drenches the altar three times, and the fire of the Lord falls and consumes sacrifice, stones, dust, and water as the people fall crying "The Lord, he is the God" — the very meaning of Elijah's name. The fourth is the still small voice (1 Kings 19): the prophet who faced 450 alone now flees in despair under a juniper tree, and God answers not with rebuke but with rest, food, a tender "What doest thou here, Elijah?", the assurance of seven thousand who have not bowed, and the call of Elisha — and after wind, earthquake, and fire, "a still small voice." The closing movement is Naboth's vineyard and Micaiah (1 Kings 21–22): Jezebel's judicial murder to seize a family inheritance and Elijah's judgment tempered by mercy when Ahab humbles himself, and the lone true prophet Micaiah against 400 court flatterers — "what the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak." And the same prophet who proved God by fire on Carmel is the prophet who returned in the Kirtland Temple (D&C 110) to restore the sealing power that binds families forever — the un-halting devotion of Carmel is exactly what the sealing power requires. Drawn from the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference (Elder D. Todd Christofferson's "Firm and Steadfast in the Faith of Christ"), Latter-day Saint scholarship (Kerry Muhlestein on "halt" as "limp"), the Journal of Discourses (Orson Pratt, 1859), the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h00m deep dive on 1 Kings 12–13; 17–22 around one ultimatum — "if the Lord be God, follow him" (1 Kings 18:21), where "halt" means to limp between two opinions. The kingdom divides under Rehoboam and Jeroboam's golden calves; God sustains Elijah by a Gentile widow at Zarephath ("make me thereof a little cake first") and raises her son; on Mount Carmel the fire of the Lord falls and Israel cries "The Lord, he is the God"; a despairing Elijah is met not with rebuke but with rest and "a still small voice"; and the week closes with Naboth's vineyard and Micaiah's integrity against 400. The prophet of Carmel is the prophet who restored the sealing power in the Kirtland Temple (D&C 110). Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 26 — 2 Samuel 11–12; 1 Kings 3; 6–9; 11: Hear Thou in Heaven Their Prayer
item.description: A 3h56m doctrinal deep dive on 2 Samuel 11–12 and 1 Kings 3; 6–9; 11 — a sustained meditation on one question: is my heart whole with God? Solomon charged Israel, "Let your heart therefore be perfect [Hebrew shalem — whole, undivided] with the Lord our God" (1 Kings 8:61), and the week is the cost of keeping that heart whole and the cost of letting it divide. Five movements. The first is David's fall (2 Samuel 11): not a single instant but a chain — a war sat out, a rooftop, a lingering look, a taking, and an escalating cover-up that ends in the murder of Uriah the Hittite, the loyal foreigner who keeps the covenant the king betrays. The second is Nathan, repentance, and the cost (2 Samuel 12; Psalm 51): the prophet's parable of the poor man's ewe lamb, "Thou art the man," David's total confession "I have sinned against the Lord," and the sober truth that the sin is put away yet the sword would not depart from his house. The third is Solomon's wisdom (1 Kings 3): asked "Ask what I shall give thee," the young king confesses "I am but a little child" and requests "an understanding heart" (Hebrew lev shomea, a hearing heart) — what we ask reveals what we treasure — even as a marriage of alliance with Egypt quietly plants the seed of his undoing. The fourth is the spine of the week, building and dedicating the temple (1 Kings 6–8; 9:1–9): stones set so silently "there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house," cherubim and palm trees carving Eden in stone and gold, the cloud of glory filling the house, and Solomon kneeling with open hands in the longest prayer in the Old Testament — "the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee," and yet "hear thou in heaven… and when thou hearest, forgive" — the appointed meeting place where a sinful people is reconciled to a holy God, accepted by the Lord: "Mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually." The closing movement is Solomon's slow turning (1 Kings 11): "But king Solomon loved many strange women" — a thousand small accommodations compounding across a lifetime until "his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God." David sinned greatly yet stayed whole; Solomon sinned subtly and came apart — and even the judgment is folded with mercy, "for David's sake," through which the Messianic promise would still come. Drawn from the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference (President Uchtdorf's "A Matter of a Few Degrees," President Nelson and President Eyring on the temple), the Old Testament Student Manual, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 3h56m deep dive on 2 Samuel 11–12 and 1 Kings 3; 6–9; 11 around one question — is my heart whole with God? David falls by a chain of choices and murders Uriah; Nathan's "Thou art the man" draws the confession "I have sinned against the Lord," yet consequence remains; Solomon asks for "an understanding heart" and builds and dedicates the temple — the spine of the week — praying "hear thou in heaven… and when thou hearest, forgive," with God's promise "mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually"; and the wisest man slowly lets his heart divide until "his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God." The standard: "Let your heart therefore be perfect with the Lord our God" (1 Kings 8:61). Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 25 — 1 Samuel 17–18; 24–26; 2 Samuel 5–7: The Battle Is the Lord's
item.description: A 4h09m doctrinal deep dive on 1 Samuel 17–18; 24–26 and 2 Samuel 5–7 — the rise of David, traced through five movements held together by one shepherd-boy's conviction: "the battle is the Lord's" (1 Samuel 17:47). The first movement is David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17): for forty days a giant defied "the armies of the living God," and Israel measured him against themselves and despaired — David measured him against God and found him small, refusing Saul's armor ("I have not proved them") and running toward the giant in the name of the Lord of Hosts, "that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel" — read with President Kimball's "The Davids and the Goliaths" (October 1974). The second is covenant friendship and envy (1 Samuel 18): the soul of Jonathan "knit with the soul of David," the crown prince stripping off robe and sword to yield his royal claim to the Lord's anointed — chesed, covenant love — set against Saul's curdling jealousy at "David his ten thousands." The third is vengeance left to the Lord (1 Samuel 24–26): twice David spares Saul ("the Lord forbid that I should… stretch forth mine hand against… the Lord's anointed"), and between them the wise Abigail intercepts David's wrath against the foolish Nabal, taking the offense upon herself and keeping him "from avenging myself with mine own hand" — Abigail read as a type of Christ the Mediator, with Sister Kristin M. Yee's "Beauty for Ashes" (April 2022). The fourth is king over Israel and the ark (2 Samuel 5–6): Zion taken and made "the city of David," David still "inquiring of the Lord" before battle, the sobering death of Uzzah who reached out to steady the ark (President David O. McKay on "steadying the ark," Conference Report, April 1936), and David dancing "before the Lord with all his might" while Michal despised him — reverence and exuberant gladness both right when offered the Lord's way. The closing movement is the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7): David would build God a house, and God instead promises to build David a house — "thy throne shall be established for ever" — the dualistic prophecy that is the seedbed of all messianic hope, fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Son of David and Eternal King. Sources span the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference (President Kimball, Sister Yee, President McKay), the Old Testament Student Manual, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Maxwell Institute, the Interpreter Foundation, the Journal of Discourses, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h09m deep dive on 1 Samuel 17–18; 24–26 and 2 Samuel 5–7. David faces Goliath with the conviction "the battle is the Lord's" (1 Samuel 17:47), refusing armor and running in the name of the Lord of Hosts; Jonathan's soul is "knit" to David's in covenant chesed while Saul's heart curdles into envy; David twice spares "the Lord's anointed" and Abigail stays his hand against Nabal — a type of Christ the Mediator; David is made king, takes Zion, and brings home the ark (Uzzah's death and "steadying the ark," David's wholehearted dance); and the Lord promises an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:16), fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David. Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 24 — 1 Samuel 8–10; 13; 15–16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart
item.description: A 3h57m doctrinal deep dive on 1 Samuel 8–10; 13; 15–16 — the story of two kings and one searching question: what is God actually looking for? Five extended sections. The first takes up Israel's demand for a king "like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8) and the Lord's piercing reply, "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them" — read alongside Mosiah 29 and the warning of "the manner of the king" who will take and take. The second follows Saul, chosen and anointed (1 Samuel 9–10): a young man searching for lost donkeys who is led by providence to Samuel, given "another heart," filled with the Spirit, then found hiding "among the stuff" — a genuine humility that makes the later fall the more sobering. The third is the failure to wait (1 Samuel 13): under pressure, with his army scattering, Saul "forced himself" and offered the burnt offering — "thou hast done foolishly" — read with President Uchtdorf's "A Matter of a Few Degrees" on how small deviations compound. The fourth is the doctrinal keystone (1 Samuel 15): commanded to destroy Amalek utterly, Saul spares Agag and the best of the flocks and calls it sacrifice, drawing Samuel's immortal answer, "to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams… rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft," and Saul's confession, "I feared the people, and obeyed their voice." The closing section is the verse that names the whole lesson (1 Samuel 16): Samuel sent to Bethlehem, son after impressive son passing by, until the Lord chooses the shepherd boy David — "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart" — the Spirit coming mightily upon David and departing from Saul. Sources span the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference (Elder Barcellos's 2025 "The Lord Looketh on the Heart," President Uchtdorf, Elder Hales, Elder Robbins), the Old Testament Student Manual, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Interpreter Foundation, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 3h57m deep dive on 1 Samuel 8–10; 13; 15–16. Israel demands a king "like all the nations" and so rejects the Lord as King; Saul is anointed and given "another heart," then unravels — he cannot wait (chapter 13, "thou hast done foolishly"), he obeys only partway and calls it sacrifice (chapter 15, "to obey is better than sacrifice"), and confesses "I feared the people." So the Lord turns to a shepherd boy in Bethlehem: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). A good beginning lost through small deviations, partial obedience, and the fear of man — and the heart God actually weighs. Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 23 — Ruth; 1 Samuel 1–7: My Heart Rejoiceth in the Lord
item.description: A 4h20m doctrinal deep dive on Ruth and 1 Samuel 1–7 — two women brought from emptiness to fullness, and a boy who learned to say "Speak, Lord." Five extended sections. The first walks the road home with Ruth — the famine that drove a family from Bethlehem ("house of bread") into Moab, Naomi's losses, and the most beautiful vow of loyalty in the Old Testament ("thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God"), built on the Hebrew chesed, covenant love. The second meets the redeemer at the gate: Boaz the go'el, the kinsman-redeemer who "buys back" lost family and raises up its name — deliverance at a price he freely pays — placing Ruth, a Gentile convert, in the lineage of Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:5), and standing as a type of the Savior our Kinsman-Redeemer. The third is Hannah's prayer and song at Shiloh — the childless wife who "poured out her soul," misjudged by Eli as drunk, who lent her son Samuel back to the Lord and sang "My heart rejoiceth in the Lord" (1 Samuel 2:1–10), the forerunner of Mary's Magnificat — set against Eli's failure with his own corrupt sons. The fourth is the doctrinal keystone: the boy Samuel learning to recognize the Lord's voice in the night, "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth," in a day when "the word of the Lord was precious." The closing section follows the ark — Israel treating it as a good-luck charm and being routed, "Ichabod, the glory is departed," the ark humbling the Philistine god Dagon, and Samuel's call to repentance at Mizpah — ending with the stone Ebenezer, "Hitherto hath the Lord helped us." Sources span the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h20m deep dive on Ruth and 1 Samuel 1–7. Ruth's vow of covenant chesed and the road from "Mara" (bitter) back to fullness, Boaz the kinsman-redeemer (go'el) as a type of Christ who places Ruth in the lineage of Jesus, Hannah pouring out her soul and singing "My heart rejoiceth in the Lord" (forerunner of Mary's Magnificat), the boy Samuel learning "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth," and the ark, Ichabod, and Samuel's Ebenezer — "Hitherto hath the Lord helped us." item.title: Doctrinal Deep Dive — From Grace to Grace: Doctrine and Covenants 93:11–20
item.description: A 4h22m doctrinal deep dive on Doctrine and Covenants 93:11–20 — the quiet, astonishing claim that even the Savior "received not of the fulness at the first, but received grace for grace," and "continued from grace to grace, until he received a fulness." Five extended sections. The first defines grace itself — the Greek charis, the Bible Dictionary's "divine means of help or strength," and the two faces of grace: redeeming grace that cleanses and forgives, and enabling grace that makes "weak things become strong" (Ether 12:27). The second traces Christ's own growth — "the child grew," "Jesus increased in wisdom and stature," and the teaching that the Son Himself grew from grace to grace. The third takes up the great misunderstanding — grace versus works — and resolves it through Ephesians 2 and James 2 and a careful reading of 2 Nephi 25:23 ("after all we can do"), with Stephen E. Robinson's parable of the bicycle and Brad Wilcox's piano-lesson analogy. The fourth follows where the pattern leads — being "glorified in me as I am in the Father" (D&C 93:20) — read alongside the earliest Christian writers (Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and the post-Nicene capstone Athanasius) and the Prophet Joseph Smith's King Follett teaching of going "from grace to grace, from exaltation to exaltation." The closing section brings it home to daily discipleship: the sacrament as weekly grace for grace, repentance as growth rather than only guilt, and the promise that slow, incremental growth is the very pattern God designed. The rare phrase "grace for grace" appears in only four places in all scripture — John 1:16, D&C 93:12, D&C 93:20, and Helaman 12:24. Sources span the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, BYU devotionals, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, and the Interpreter Foundation.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h22m deep dive on D&C 93:11–20 — "from grace to grace." What grace is (redeeming and enabling), how even Christ "increased" and grew grace for grace, the grace-and-works question resolved through Ephesians 2, James 2, and 2 Nephi 25:23 ("after all we can do") with Robinson's bicycle parable and Wilcox's piano analogy, where the pattern leads — being "glorified… as I am in the Father" — read with the earliest Christian writers and Joseph Smith's King Follett sermon, and what it means for daily discipleship. Drawn from the full Gospel Library.

item.title: CFM Week 22 — Judges 2–4; 6–8; 13–16: The Cycle and the Deliverers
item.description: A 4h17m doctrinal deep dive on Judges 2–4; 6–8; 13–16 — the most honest book in the Old Testament about how people drift from God, and the most hopeful about how He keeps coming back for them. Five extended sections. The first lays down the cycle of Judges 2 — rest, forgetting, bondage, crying out, deliverance, relapse — the same wheel that turns through the Book of Mormon as the pride cycle. The second tells of Deborah, Barak, and Jael, with Sisera's nine hundred chariots of iron bogged down at the river Kishon and the reminder that "the Lord is gone out before thee." The third is the heart of the book: Gideon, the "least" of his family greeted as a "mighty man of valour," his altar Jehovah-shalom, the sign of the fleece, and an army shrunk from 32,000 to just 300 "lest Israel vaunt themselves," followed by his noble refusal of a crown. The fourth follows Samson — the Nazarite vow set on him before birth, his Spirit-given strength squandered compromise by compromise until "he wist not that the Lord was departed from him," and a death that brought a greater deliverance than his life. The closing section ties every flawed and partial deliverer to the perfect and final Deliverer, Jesus Christ — reading Gideon's fleece, Jael's victory, and Samson through the eyes of the earliest Christian writers — and grounds it all in the promise that the Lord makes "weak things become strong" (Ether 12:27). Sources span the full Gospel Library — General Conference, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers (Irenaeus, Lactantius, Hippolytus, Tertullian), the Interpreter Foundation, Latter-day Saint scholarship, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h17m deep dive on Judges 2–4; 6–8; 13–16. The cycle of Judges 2 (the same wheel as the Book of Mormon's pride cycle), Deborah and Jael against Sisera's iron chariots, Gideon's army cut to 300 "lest Israel vaunt themselves," Samson's Nazarite vow and the death that delivered more than his life, and the thread that ties every flawed deliverer to the perfect One — Jesus Christ — grounded in "weak things become strong" (Ether 12:27).

item.title: CFM Week 21 — Joshua 1–8; 23–24: Be Strong and of a Good Courage
item.description: A 4h37m doctrinal deep dive on Joshua 1–8; 23–24. Five extended sections trace the commission of Joshua (Yehoshua / Yeshua — the same name as Jesus) and the "I will not fail thee" promise rooted in Deuteronomy 31; Rahab the Canaanite whose scarlet cord becomes a Passover-and-cross type (Justin Martyr, Origen, Aphrahat) and lands her in the genealogy of Christ; the crossing of the Jordan and the fall of Jericho read as baptismal and conquest typology, with a five-layer treatment of the herem ("utter destruction") problem; Joshua's farewell covenant at Shechem in its ancient suzerain-vassal treaty form, with the binary "Choose you this day" call; and a closing section on living the covenant day to day. Sources span the full Gospel Library — General Conference, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, BYU Studies, the Maxwell Institute, and the Interpreter Foundation.

item.title: CFM Week 20 — Deuteronomy 6–8; 15; 18; 29–30; 34: Moses' Farewell on the Plains of Moab
item.description: A one-hour-forty-minute deep dive on Moses' farewell sermon. Seven sections trace the most theologically concentrated chapters in the Old Testament: the Shema (Deut 6), the great commandment to love God with all thy heart, the lesson of the manna (Deut 8) that Christ would quote in the wilderness, the year of release and debt forgiveness (Deut 15), the prophecy of a prophet like unto Moses (Deut 18) pointing forward to Christ and Joseph Smith, the sweeping blessings and cursings of the covenant (Deut 29–30), Moses' invitation to "choose life," and finally the death of Moses on Pisgah (Deut 34) — a death so unique that the Bible says no man knows the place of his burial, and Latter-day Saints have something more to say about that.
